# Probability, diffusion, and long tails {#sec-foundations}

## From a trajectory to an ensemble

A stochastic model describes many possible trajectories, not an uncertain value of one predetermined trajectory. Let $X(t)$ be a particle's position. Its probability density $P(x,t)$ is defined by $\Pr\{x<X(t)<x+dx\}=P(x,t)dx$. When point masses occur, it is more precise to speak of a probability measure: $a\delta(x-x_*)$ means a probability $a$ exactly at $x_*$. The density must satisfy

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}P(x,t)\,dx=1.
$$ {#eq-found-normalization}

The ensemble mean is $\langle X(t)\rangle=\int xP(x,t)dx$. The mean squared displacement (MSD) is $\langle[X(t)-X(0)]^2\rangle$. It equals the variance only when the mean displacement vanishes. In the symmetric models here $X(0)=0$ and $\langle X(t)\rangle=0$, so the distinction disappears. It returns immediately in a field or chemotactic gradient.

A propagator is the distribution generated by an initially localized particle. If independent walkers start with density $P_0$, spatial translation invariance gives $P(x,t)=\int G(x-y,t)P_0(y)dy$. This superposition requires linear, noninteracting transport. Exclusion, alignment, or density-dependent motility can invalidate it.

## Why ordinary diffusion is so common

Consider independent identically distributed jumps $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n$ with mean zero and finite variance $\sigma^2$. The sum $S_n=\sum_j\xi_j$ has variance $n\sigma^2$. The central limit theorem says that the distribution of $S_n/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ approaches a unit Gaussian as $n\to\infty$. It does not say that every finite-time tail is Gaussian, nor that the theorem applies when the variance is infinite.

For nearest-neighbor steps $\pm a$ at intervals $\Delta t$, probability conservation gives

$$
P(x,t+\Delta t)=\tfrac12P(x-a,t)+\tfrac12P(x+a,t).
$$

Taylor expansion yields $\Delta t\,\partial_tP=(a^2/2)\partial_x^2P$ to leading order. In a continuum limit with $D=a^2/(2\Delta t)$ fixed,

$$
\partial_tP=D\partial_x^2P,\qquad
G(x,t)=\frac{\exp[-x^2/(4Dt)]}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}},\qquad
\langle X^2(t)\rangle=2Dt.
$$ {#eq-found-diffusion}

The Gaussian normalization follows by the substitution $u=x/\sqrt{4Dt}$. Its variance follows by differentiating the Gaussian integral with respect to its width, or by integrating the diffusion equation against $x^2$. Boundary terms vanish on the infinite line for a decaying solution.

The Gaussian is positive at every finite $x$ for every $t>0$. This is an approximation on diffusive length and time scales. It cannot impose an exact maximum microscopic propagation speed. A finite-speed random walk can have this Gaussian central limit while its true distribution is exactly zero outside a moving boundary. This observation motivates persistent walks before any heavy tails are introduced.

## Tails, survival, and what diverges

We will often use the Lomax law

$$
\psi(\tau)=\frac{\gamma}{\tau_0}
\left(1+\frac{\tau}{\tau_0}\right)^{-1-\gamma},\qquad
\Psi(t)=\int_t^\infty\psi(\tau)d\tau=
\left(1+\frac{t}{\tau_0}\right)^{-\gamma}.
$$ {#eq-found-lomax}

Here $\psi$ has units of inverse time and $\Psi$ is dimensionless. The survival describes the probability that a flight which has just begun lasts longer than $t$. It is not the probability density of a renewal at $t$.

Integrating by parts gives a useful moment formula,

$$
\langle\tau^q\rangle=q\int_0^\infty t^{q-1}\Psi(t)dt
=\tau_0^q\frac{\Gamma(q+1)\Gamma(\gamma-q)}{\Gamma(\gamma)},
\quad 0<q<\gamma.
$$ {#eq-found-duration-moments}

The beta integral proves the last equality: set $u=t/\tau_0$ and use $\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}(1+u)^{-a-b}du=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)$. At infinity the integrand behaves as $t^{q-1-\gamma}$, so convergence requires $q<\gamma$. In particular,

$$
\mu=\langle\tau\rangle=\frac{\tau_0}{\gamma-1}\quad(\gamma>1),\qquad
\langle\tau^2\rangle=\frac{2\tau_0^2}{(\gamma-1)(\gamma-2)}\quad(\gamma>2).
$$

An infinite expectation does not mean an infinite observed duration. Every draw is finite with probability one; the expectation fails because progressively rarer, larger draws keep contributing to the integral. A finite sample always has a largest value. Increasing the sample size can change that value enough to destabilize the sample mean.

The hazard rate $\lambda(a)=\psi(a)/\Psi(a)$ is the conditional probability per unit time that a surviving flight ends at age $a$. For the Lomax law, $\lambda(a)=\gamma/(\tau_0+a)$. Old flights are less likely to end in the next short interval than newly started ones. For an exponential law $\psi(\tau)=re^{-r\tau}$ the hazard is the constant $r$. This distinction is the microscopic source of memory.

::: {.callout-note}
## Density and survival slopes
For a tail $\psi(\tau)\propto\tau^{-1-\gamma}$, a plot of the survival on logarithmic axes has slope $-\gamma$. A density histogram has slope $-1-\gamma$. Logarithmic binning changes bin widths, so raw counts must be divided by their widths before interpreting them as a density.
:::

## Fourier and Laplace transforms as bookkeeping

Our conventions are

$$
\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{ikx}f(x)dx,\qquad
\widetilde g(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}g(t)dt,\qquad \Re s>0.
$$ {#eq-found-transforms}

When there is no ambiguity we write $P(k,s)$ for both transforms. The characteristic function $P(k,t)$ obeys $P(0,t)=1$. Its derivatives give moments when those moments exist: $\langle X^n\rangle=i^{-n}\partial_k^nP(k,t)|_{k=0}$. Thus $\langle X^2\rangle=-\partial_k^2P|_0$. Spatial convolution becomes multiplication because $e^{ik(x+y)}=e^{ikx}e^{iky}$. The same argument applies to causal time convolutions with $e^{-st}$.

Three identities will do most of the work:

$$
\widetilde\Psi(s)=\frac{1-\widetilde\psi(s)}s,\qquad
\mathcal L[t^{a-1}](s)=\Gamma(a)s^{-a}\quad(a>0),\qquad
\mathcal{FL}\{f(t)\delta(x-vt)\}=\widetilde f(s-ikv).
$$ {#eq-found-identities}

The first identity follows by swapping the integrals in $\int_0^\infty e^{-st}\int_t^\infty\psi(u)dudt$. The second follows by $u=st$. The third follows by evaluating the spatial integral first. Its combination $s-ikv$ expresses advection along a trajectory; it is the source of space–time coupling in Lévy walks.

## Stable distributions and the generalized central limit theorem

Suppose symmetric jumps have characteristic function

$$
\widehat f(k)=1-c|k|^\alpha+o(|k|^\alpha),\quad
0<\alpha<2,\quad c>0.
$$

For $S_n/n^{1/\alpha}$ the characteristic function is $[\widehat f(k/n^{1/\alpha})]^n\to e^{-c|k|^\alpha}$. This limit defines a symmetric stable law. The ordinary Gaussian corresponds to $\alpha=2$; the Cauchy density $a/[\pi(x^2+a^2)]$ has transform $e^{-a|k|}$ and corresponds to $\alpha=1$. A stable law is called stable because sums of independent copies have the same shape after rescaling.

The inverse Fourier formula is

$$
L_\alpha(x;c)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ikx-c|k|^\alpha}dk.
$$

It need not have an elementary closed form. For $0<\alpha<2$ its tails decay as $|x|^{-1-\alpha}$, and absolute moments exist only for orders $q<\alpha$. One can see the moment restriction directly by comparing $\int^\infty x^q x^{-1-\alpha}dx$ with a power integral. Nonanalyticity of $|k|^\alpha$ at $k=0$ is another expression of the failure of sufficiently high moments.

The generalized central limit theorem requires a suitable tail domain of attraction, not merely an attractive straight line over a short range of a log plot. Asymmetry introduces skew stable laws; temporal dependence can invalidate independent-sum reasoning. We restrict to symmetric independent increments whenever using this elementary argument.

## Continuous-time random walks

Let a particle wait for $\tau_1$, jump by $\xi_1$, wait for $\tau_2$, and continue. Assume all waiting times are iid with density $\psi$ and all jumps iid with density $f$, independent of the waits. At observation time $t$, the number of completed jumps is random. This continuous-time random walk (CTRW) was developed into a transform method by Montroll and Weiss [@montroll1965].

Define the arrival density $Q(x,t)$ to count arrivals immediately after jumps, including $\delta(x)\delta(t)$ at the start. Its renewal equation is

$$
Q(x,t)=\delta(x)\delta(t)+\int_0^t d\tau\int_{\mathbb R}dy\,
\psi(\tau)f(y)Q(x-y,t-\tau).
$$

An arriving particle remains where it is until the next jump. Therefore $P(x,t)=\int_0^t\Psi(\tau)Q(x,t-\tau)d\tau$. Transforming these two equations gives

$$
P(k,s)=\frac{1-\widetilde\psi(s)}{s[1-\widetilde\psi(s)\widehat f(k)]}.
$$ {#eq-found-montroll-weiss}

The numerator is an occupation factor for the unfinished waiting interval. Omitting it destroys normalization. Indeed $P(0,s)=1/s$ follows exactly from this expression.

If $\mu<\infty$ and $\sigma^2<\infty$, expand $\widetilde\psi(s)=1-\mu s+o(s)$ and $\widehat f(k)=1-\sigma^2k^2/2+o(k^2)$. At diffusive scales $s\sim k^2$, @eq-found-montroll-weiss becomes $(s+Dk^2)^{-1}$ with $D=\sigma^2/(2\mu)$. Inverting recovers @eq-found-diffusion.

If the waiting mean diverges and $1-\widetilde\psi(s)\sim b s^\beta$, $0<\beta<1$, while the jump variance remains finite, then

$$
P(k,s)\simeq\frac{s^{\beta-1}}{s^\beta+Kk^2},\qquad
K=\frac{\sigma^2}{2b},\qquad
\langle X^2(t)\rangle\simeq\frac{2K}{\Gamma(1+\beta)}t^\beta.
$$ {#eq-found-subdiffusion}

Here $\beta$ labels a waiting-time tail; we reserve $\gamma$ for the moving-flight tail later. Long immobile waits cause subdiffusion. Conversely, finite mean waits and stable jumps give $P(k,s)\simeq(s+K_\alpha|k|^\alpha)^{-1}$ and $P(k,t)=e^{-K_\alpha t|k|^\alpha}$. This is a Lévy **flight**. Its jumps are instantaneous and its variance is infinite for $\alpha<2$.

Allowing both kinds of tails produces $s^{\beta-1}/(s^\beta+K|k|^\alpha)$ and typical width $t^{\beta/\alpha}$. This is a statement about uncoupled waits and jumps. Simply substituting $\alpha=\gamma$ into it does not derive a finite-speed walk.

## Fractional diffusion without mysterious notation

The Caputo derivative for $0<\beta<1$ is

$$
{}^C D_t^\beta f(t)=\frac1{\Gamma(1-\beta)}
\int_0^t(t-u)^{-\beta}f'(u)du.
$$

Its Laplace transform is $s^\beta\widetilde f-s^{\beta-1}f(0)$. Define the fractional Laplacian through its Fourier symbol $\mathcal F[(-\partial_x^2)^{\alpha/2}f]=|k|^\alpha\widehat f$. Then the uncoupled long-time equation is

$$
{}^C D_t^\beta P=-K(-\partial_x^2)^{\alpha/2}P.
$$

This notation abbreviates a memory integral and a spatially nonlocal operator; it does not change the stochastic construction. Initial terms depend on the definition of fractional derivative. A Riemann–Liouville derivative has different initial bookkeeping. The transform equation is often the safest way to specify which convention is meant. A space-fractional diffusion equation still has arbitrarily distant jumps and cannot by itself enforce $|X(t)|\le vt$.

## Exercises

1. Derive the survival and mean of an exponential duration law. Explain why observing that a flight has already lasted a long time does not change its remaining lifetime distribution.
2. Show that truncating a symmetric $|x|^{-1-\alpha}$ jump law at a large length $L$ makes its variance finite. Estimate how that variance grows with $L$ for $\alpha<2$.
3. Starting from @eq-found-montroll-weiss, derive the MSD in @eq-found-subdiffusion without inverting the full density.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked solutions
1. $\Psi(t)=e^{-rt}$ and $\langle\tau\rangle=\int_0^\infty\Psi(t)dt=1/r$. Conditional survival is $\Psi(a+t)/\Psi(a)=e^{-rt}$, independent of age $a$. This is the memoryless property.

2. The tail contribution is proportional to $\int^{L}x^{1-\alpha}dx\propto L^{2-\alpha}/(2-\alpha)$. At fixed finite $L$, an eventual Gaussian central limit is possible; its onset can be very late as $L$ increases. Taking $L\to\infty$ before the long-time limit is different from taking it afterward.

3. Expand $P(k,s)=s^{-1}[1-Kk^2/s^\beta+O(k^4)]$. Then $-\partial_k^2P|_0=2Ks^{-1-\beta}$. Use $\mathcal L^{-1}s^{-1-\beta}=t^\beta/\Gamma(1+\beta)$.
:::
